businesses.name: GAURANFUCKING TEA
businesses.category: Tea shop and VHS ad counter
businesses.tagline: We guarantee you'll like it, or else fuck you.
businesses.description: A cheerful tea counter with the least reassuring guarantee on the block. Lin performs the slogan outside while Mara and Eli keep the actual service warmer than the advertising.
businesses.backstory: Mara rented a small counter and recorded a rough commercial to make it look established. The tape’s awkward pause before the guarantee became the part everyone quoted. Now people arrive to make her say the line, film their friends reacting, and argue about whether a satisfaction promise can sound like a threat. Lin turned that embarrassment into a deliberate street performance. Eli made the menu small enough that the shop could still serve what it advertised. Their recurring problem is simple: the louder the ad gets, the harder it is to hear what a customer actually wants. Mara’s test is to honor a real complaint while the whole block expects another punch line.
ads: We guarantee you'll like it, or else fuck you.
NOW WITH A PAUSE LONG ENOUGH TO RECONSIDER THE SLOGAN.
PressureTV special: one cup, three takes, zero indoor voices.

interior.style: Warm counter, tea tins, and a deliberately overplayed VHS monitor
interior.description: A compact tasting counter faces a shelf of fictional tins. A small television loops ad cards. Plain text signs carry the joke; no recovered logo is imitated.

businesses.name: Hordash
businesses.description: An adult escort dispatch satire where the customer-service problem is usually a customer assuming the app has booked an entire human being.
businesses.backstory: Nadia opened an office because a contact button was being mistaken for an answer to every question. Tasha wanted a place to finish a shift without being scored by somebody who had ordered the wrong thing. Ren wanted the word available to refer to a person’s decision rather than a green dot. Their arguments are about schedules, refunds, false certainty, and an app that calls every delay a premium experience. The office makes no attempt to hide the adult premise, but its front counter sells clothing, stickers, and empty prop bags. The people behind the logo are witty, impatient, and competent, even when a customer expects them to be just an app notification. The recurring city situation is a mislabeled promotional vehicle booking that several shops think is theirs.
ads: YOUR EVENING HAS BEEN REASSIGNED. Same shoes. Different expectations.
A premium fee for a basic misunderstanding.
Five stars for the outfit. One star for your reading comprehension.

interior.style: After-hours dispatch desk with playful delivery-app signage
interior.description: A bright bookings desk, coat hooks, and a whiteboard of fictional shifts. Interactions stay at the front desk; the shop offers virtual merchandise.

businesses.name: Mike Hawk Campaign Office
businesses.tagline: Long on commitment. Hard on excuses.
businesses.description: Mike and his two recruits roam the commercial sidewalks, making every pitch sound suggestive while arguing over actual neighborhood problems.
businesses.backstory: Mike built his campaign around the conviction that nobody forgets a promise if it sounds a little inappropriate. That leaves Ada translating his speeches into ordinary requests and Noah trying to get a budget sentence through the slogan printer. Their office has a pothole map, a volunteer kettle, and stacks of posters awaiting increasingly questionable revisions. Mike wants the block to see him everywhere. Ada wants one shopkeeper to feel listened to. Noah wants somebody to read page two. The three can agree that a broken street needs fixing; they cannot agree on how to say it without the crowd laughing. Their next big campaign moment begins with a small problem: their own signs have blocked Mara’s loading space. Ada wants them moved before anybody announces another initiative.
ads: MIKE HAWK: I stand with my people long and hard on these topics.
A stronger platform. A longer commitment. Please read the policy.
Mike Hawk wants to fill the holes in this city. Public Works would appreciate a date.

interior.description: Poster stacks surround a folding table and a pothole map. Mike, Ada, and Noah are usually outside canvassing; their merchandise counter remains inspectable.

businesses.name: Robbery 1s Exchange
businesses.description: June checks receipts, Leo repairs sneakers, and Samira records the stories people attach to them. The shop sells clearly labeled fictional replicas.
businesses.backstory: A story about dangerous shoes became easier to retell than to document. June built the Exchange around that gap: every incoming pair gets a condition note, every claim gets a source, and every replica gets a label. Leo soon discovered that customers would pay attention to a supposed curse before they noticed excellent stitching. Samira made room for the stories without making them certificates of truth. The Drop Watch and Designer Kicks share a crowded retail noticeboard. June leaves the original-pair plinth empty until she can explain exactly what belongs there. The empty space irritates Hugo, who thinks every surface should make a sale; Samira thinks it might be the most honest exhibit on the block.
ads: FRESH SOLES. QUESTIONABLE HISTORY. Receipts welcome.
The replica is labeled. The confidence is authentic.
The Drop Watch board: late releases, early opinions.

interior.style: Repair bench, shoe display, and conflicting-story noticeboard
interior.description: Replicas sit apart from an empty story-display plinth. A repair counter and zine rack make the shop useful without declaring custody of the original shoes.

businesses.name: Hitman Gear
businesses.description: A fiercely serious film-gear boutique where Plot Armor is a vest, a threat is probably a lighting note, and nobody can find the batteries.
businesses.backstory: Vik learned that a client who ignored a practical lighting suggestion would listen if it sounded like the beginning of an operation. Marisol gave that absurd confidence a wardrobe. Owen supplied the noise. Together they made a shop that looks ready for a cinematic confrontation and spends most of its time discussing return dates, fabric, and missing adapters. Their products are fictional costume pieces and production props, with no weapons or claims of protective performance. The block treats the shop as the place to get ready for a big entrance. The staff treats every big entrance as another chance for somebody to forget the deposit. Their continuing dispute with RealCameraMen is over whose tiny practical contribution saved the shoot.
ads: PLOT ARMOR. Great silhouette. Absolutely no plot guarantees.
You bring the tension. Owen brings the empty biscuit tin.
A serious look for a very unserious budget.

interior.style: Compact film wardrobe and prop counter
interior.description: Garment rails, a clapboard shelf, and harmless sound props face the shop counter. There are no functional weapons on sale.

businesses.name: RealCameraMen
businesses.category: Camera hot takes and production studio
businesses.tagline: Your lens is innocent. Your quote is not.
businesses.description: A production counter whose straight-faced equipment manifestos get louder whenever the client asks for a discount.
businesses.backstory: Zofia could explain why a camera choice mattered in thirty seconds. The problem was that the block preferred the version where she pretended the wrong memory card was a moral failure. Cleo gave those monologues a setting, and Kwame started scheduling them between paid jobs. Their public persona announces ridiculous rules about lenses, LUTs, gimbals, batteries, and who is allowed to call themselves professional. In quieter conversations the same staff solve practical problems with whatever works. Who Did the Shoot? supplies the recurring production dispute: several people can prove they contributed, but nobody can agree which contribution the invoice should celebrate. Their professionalism and their ridiculous advertising coexist; the joke does not require the crew to be incompetent.
ads: REAL CAMERAMEN DO NOT RUN OUT OF BATTERY. We call it an intentional ending.
Who Did the Shoot? Everybody submitted a deposit request.
Thirty seconds of lens philosophy. Forty-five minutes of invoice discussion.

interior.style: Small practical studio with a grandiose hot-take wall
interior.description: A simple set, a camera-prop shelf, and a production counter surround handwritten equipment rules. The rules contradict one another on purpose.

businesses.name: PressureTV Network
businesses.description: A local entertainment studio where tiny block events get huge headlines and every sponsor thinks it owns the commercial break.
businesses.backstory: Darnell can make a delayed kettle sound like a developing emergency. Priya can find out who unplugged it. Hugo can sell the kettle company a response segment before either of them has finished. That is the studio’s daily rhythm. The studio’s entertainment desk faces the street, which makes ignoring an annoyed neighbor almost impossible. A programming board lists Diamond Girls Radio and its Nigeria/Ghana focus under Diamond Girls x McCluster Network. PRIM3.exe sits in the programming notes while Priya waits for a description she can actually schedule. The central conflict is proximity: everybody covered by the studio can walk over and complain, and everybody buying an ad still expects to be called a friend.

Diamond Girls Radio on the programming board. Turn the block up.
Exclusive sponsorship available. Please define exclusive before paying.

businesses.name: Baddies on Wheels
businesses.tagline: The entrance is part of the ride.
businesses.description: A driver-led vehicle-media business where dispatch, maintenance, and presentation have to fit in the same working day.
businesses.backstory: Amina likes a beautiful arrival but measures a good day by everyone getting where they agreed to go. Tomas knows how quickly a filmed entrance can become tomorrow’s repair job. Beatrice remembers the appointment before the client remembers making it. Their brand celebrates vehicles and personalities, combining promotional work with a small service relationship to the Whip garage. The recurring mistake is assuming that a shiny van on camera is a spare van in the schedule. A promotional booking links them to Hordash and RealCameraMen, whose descriptions sound alike until someone asks what must actually be carried. Their souvenir ride pass looks glamorous enough that Beatrice has to remind visitors it belongs on a shelf; the actual schedule remains on her desk, where adjectives cannot change it.
ads: THE ENTRANCE IS PART OF THE RIDE. Being on time is the other part.
Baddies on Wheels: main-character energy, scheduled maintenance.
Your appearance has a booking. Your luggage should have a description.

npcs.name: Mara Costa
npcs.role: Owner and reluctant face of the guarantee
npcs.backstory: Mara grew up helping a relative run a neighborhood snack counter in Recife, where remembering an order mattered more than having a slogan. Years later she opened the city shop with a small menu and borrowed recording equipment. One furious practice take became the commercial everybody wanted. She is proud of the attention and embarrassed that people sometimes leave quoting the ad without remembering the tea. Mara keeps a notebook of regulars’ preferences behind the till and quietly replaces drinks customers dislike. Her ambition is to make the guarantee honest without becoming a bland version of herself. She trusts Eli with the stock and Lin with the performance; she needs both of them to tell her when she has confused being memorable with being right.
npcs.personality: Blunt, hospitable, ambitious, and capable of apologizing without losing her nerve.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome. The tea is hot. The guarantee is unnecessarily personal.

topics.label: Explain that guarantee.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So what happens if I don’t like the tea?

lines.speaker: Mara Costa
lines.text: I make you another one. I run a shop, not a hostage situation.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Your sign has a different energy.

lines.speaker: Mara Costa
lines.text: We guarantee you'll like it, or else fuck you.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: There it is.

lines.speaker: Mara Costa
lines.text: And there’s the kettle. One of those things actually solves your problem.

topics.label: How did the VHS ad happen?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did you deliberately make the ad look thirty years old?

lines.speaker: Mara Costa
lines.text: At first? No. That was the camera we had.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And the dramatic zoom?

lines.speaker: Mara Costa
lines.text: The table moved. Cleo called it a creative decision, then sent an invoice.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did the ad work?

lines.speaker: Mara Costa
lines.text: People know every word. Now I’m trying the radical next step of selling them tea.

topics.label: What do you want from this block?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: PressureTV says you’re taking over the neighborhood.

lines.speaker: Mara Costa
lines.text: I asked for a thirty-second commercial. Hugo sold me an era.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You don’t want an empire?

lines.speaker: Mara Costa
lines.text: I want Eli to get a lunch break and Lin to stop shouting at delivery drivers.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds smaller.

lines.speaker: Mara Costa
lines.text: It sounds achievable. Buy a cup and we can fund the revolution slowly.

dialogue.farewell: Come back. Tell me what you actually liked this time.

npcs.name: Lin Qiao
npcs.backstory: Lin worked backstage on small performances in Hangzhou before deciding she preferred the moment when an audience could answer back. She moved to the city with a habit of studying timing: when a passerby looks up, when a joke needs silence, when a sales pitch should end. Mara’s ad gave her an unusually rude line to perform with perfect composure. She knows the guarantee sounds absurd and makes that awareness part of the act. Off the pavement she is quieter, rehearsing her own short comedy pieces and helping Eli move crates. Her conflict is with being remembered only as the person who says the slogan. She wants to direct the next commercial and make the whole shop take her ideas as seriously as her ability to draw a crowd.
npcs.personality: Observant, playful, self-possessed; a performer rather than an accent joke.

dialogue.greeting: You heard the slogan from across the street. That means I’m doing my job.

topics.label: Give me the full pitch.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: All right. Sell me the tea.

lines.speaker: Lin Qiao
lines.text: We guarantee you'll like it, or else fuck you.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s your customer-service voice?

lines.speaker: Lin Qiao
lines.text: No. My customer-service voice asks whether you want the lid on.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Lid on, then.

lines.speaker: Lin Qiao
lines.text: Excellent. We’ve built a relationship without even calling security.

topics.label: Why does everyone stop for you?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You make that line sound almost polite.

lines.speaker: Lin Qiao
lines.text: The pause does the work. You need time to think the guarantee is normal.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Then you ruin it.

lines.speaker: Lin Qiao
lines.text: Then I reveal the product. That is a theatrical distinction.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Ever want to perform something else?

lines.speaker: Lin Qiao
lines.text: Yes. My next production includes a chair and a scene where nobody asks me to shout.

topics.label: What do you think of Mike Hawk?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Mike’s recruiters are competing with your pitch.

lines.speaker: Lin Qiao
lines.text: Ada and I have an agreement. Tea first, civic disappointment second.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And Mike?

lines.speaker: Lin Qiao
lines.text: He said he could go all day. I asked him to cover my afternoon break.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did he?

lines.speaker: Lin Qiao
lines.text: He made a statement supporting breaks. Mara is still waiting for the actual person.

dialogue.farewell: Try the tea. If you quote me, at least get the timing right.

npcs.name: Eli Mensah
npcs.backstory: Eli learned stock work in Accra and developed a private affection for lists that solve actual problems. After moving to the city he took a temporary job counting tea tins and stayed because Mara would admit when his quiet corrections saved a disastrous promotion. He knows which customers really enjoy a limited edition and which only want to photograph the sign. He is neither the shop’s stern parent nor its silent background helper: he makes dry jokes, has strong opinions about the playlist, and refuses to hide behind a clipboard. He wants a tasting evening where customers can disagree without becoming content. His obstacle is that Hugo keeps calling every modest idea a launch, and Mara sometimes believes him long enough to order too many cups.
npcs.personality: Patient, exact, dryly funny; enjoys useful systems and unhurried conversation.

dialogue.greeting: If you want the ad, Lin is outside. If you want a recommendation, tell me what you like.

topics.label: What is actually good here?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you recommend?

lines.speaker: Eli Mensah
lines.text: Something you will finish. The biggest cup is not a personality test.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Mara said everything was guaranteed.

lines.speaker: Eli Mensah
lines.text: Mara handles certainty. I handle stock.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Those ever disagree?

lines.speaker: Eli Mensah
lines.text: Every Friday. Certainty has never carried a crate upstairs.

topics.label: Why is everything limited edition?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is this tin genuinely limited?

lines.speaker: Eli Mensah
lines.text: We have six. That is a limit, yes.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The poster makes it sound historic.

lines.speaker: Eli Mensah
lines.text: Hugo put FINAL CHANCE on a product that had not arrived yet.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What happened?

lines.speaker: Eli Mensah
lines.text: We had a first chance the next morning. Nobody issued a correction.

topics.label: Tell me about your tasting night.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What would you do with the shop for one evening?

lines.speaker: Eli Mensah
lines.text: Small cups. Actual questions. No one yelling a slogan over the answers.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Would Lin agree?

lines.speaker: Eli Mensah
lines.text: She asked whether silence counts as a paid performance. I said yes.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And Mara?

lines.speaker: Eli Mensah
lines.text: She’s worried people might dislike something. I told her that’s when a guarantee gets interesting.

dialogue.farewell: Enjoy it. An honest opinion is more useful than a five-star reflex.

npcs.name: Nadia Vale
npcs.backstory: Nadia spent years arranging nightlife schedules in Lisbon and learned that a clear question prevents more trouble than a confident promise. In the city she opened Hordash’s dispatch desk after watching customers treat a loading icon as consent to everything they imagined. She keeps an old paper diary beside the brightly branded screen because the diary has never announced that a person is arriving before the person has agreed to leave. Her wit is brisk, but she is affectionate toward the people who work with her. She wants a week where the bookings mean what they say. Tasha respects her boundaries; Ren insists that Nadia apply the same patience to herself. The recurring vehicle mix-up tests whether she can ask for help before her whole shift becomes everybody else’s emergency.
npcs.personality: Fast, practical, dry; asks precise questions and hates decorative certainty.

dialogue.greeting: Before you tell me the app said five minutes, tell me what you actually ordered.

topics.label: Why does the ETA keep changing?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: It said five minutes twenty minutes ago.

lines.speaker: Nadia Vale
lines.text: That was emotional distance. Geography has submitted a correction.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So what am I paying the premium fee for?

lines.speaker: Nadia Vale
lines.text: A larger version of the same apology.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can you give me an honest answer?

lines.speaker: Nadia Vale
lines.text: Yes. Ask a person before you trust a spinning circle.

topics.label: What does this office actually do?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The name suggests you can deliver anything.

lines.speaker: Nadia Vale
lines.text: The name suggests our marketing department needs supervision.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So you arrange nightlife bookings?

lines.speaker: Nadia Vale
lines.text: With actual adults who decide their own availability. Shocking business model.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And this counter?

lines.speaker: Nadia Vale
lines.text: Merchandise. The empty bag is twenty-one credits. Your assumptions cost extra elsewhere.

topics.label: Why are three shops asking about one van?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Amina says you borrowed her promotional booking.

lines.speaker: Nadia Vale
lines.text: I booked a vehicle for a night-shift promo. Kwame booked a promo with a night vehicle.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds almost identical.

lines.speaker: Nadia Vale
lines.text: Exactly. Everyone read the adjective and skipped the noun.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What would fix it?

lines.speaker: Nadia Vale
lines.text: Ask who is driving, what is being carried, and where it must go. Then write the answers down.

dialogue.farewell: Read the description. It’s the least expensive part of the experience.

npcs.name: Tasha Bell
npcs.backstory: Tasha grew up in New Haven and has held enough service jobs to recognize the smile people expect when they are being unreasonable. She now works as an adult entertainer and sometimes carries promotional orders between the district’s shops, arranging her own shifts through Nadia. She is proud of her performance skills and protective of the time when she is simply a neighbor buying tea. Her public ratings annoy her because they turn wildly different expectations into the same five stars. She enjoys the road, knows the block’s shortcuts, and keeps a notebook of comedy observations for a possible radio appearance. Her next step is a paid hosting segment with PressureTV, where she wants to tell the story herself instead of appearing as somebody else’s punch line.
npcs.personality: Quick, funny, independent, and generous with people who ask instead of presume.

dialogue.greeting: If this is about a rating, I hope you rated your own behavior first.

topics.label: What is your worst review?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Somebody gave you one star for being early?

lines.speaker: Tasha Bell
lines.text: He said it put pressure on him to be ready. Being late would have ruined his evening.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So there was no winning.

lines.speaker: Tasha Bell
lines.text: There was. I finished the shift and bought tea.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did you answer him?

lines.speaker: Tasha Bell
lines.text: I drafted a beautiful reply. Nadia reminded me that silence can also be a refund to my nervous system.

topics.label: What do you do off shift?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you ever stop doing the sales pitch?

lines.speaker: Tasha Bell
lines.text: Sure. This is my regular voice. No subscription required.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What are you writing in that notebook?

lines.speaker: Tasha Bell
lines.text: Stories. People get very original when they think they’re the first person to be rude.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: PressureTV material?

lines.speaker: Tasha Bell
lines.text: Maybe. First I need Hugo to understand that exposure is not a hosting fee.

topics.label: Who knows this block best?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who should I ask for directions?

lines.speaker: Tasha Bell
lines.text: Beatrice if you want to arrive. Mike if you want to hear how committed he is to arriving.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What about you?

lines.speaker: Tasha Bell
lines.text: I’ll give you the route and tell you which tea line is shortest.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s a premium service.

lines.speaker: Tasha Bell
lines.text: Exactly. Now watch an app charge you for the same information with a worse attitude.

dialogue.farewell: Take care. If the story is about me, let me finish the sentence.

npcs.name: Ren Okafor
npcs.backstory: Ren worked customer support in Lagos before arriving in the city and becoming the person everyone asks to make confusing instructions sound human. At Hordash they handle bookings, disputes, and the gap between a customer’s imagination and the actual agreement. They have a mischievous love of formal language and sometimes read a ridiculous complaint as if it were a prestigious literary work. Behind the jokes is a practical goal: a shift that ends when it is supposed to end. Ren likes helping Tasha develop her on-air voice and has started keeping a list of app phrases that mean nothing. They want Nadia to print one honest poster, even if it has to say that somebody does not know the answer yet.
npcs.personality: Calm, sharp, theatrical with paperwork; protective of clear agreements.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome to support. Start with the part that happened, then we’ll discuss the part you expected.

topics.label: What is the usual misunderstanding?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do people get wrong most often?

lines.speaker: Ren Okafor
lines.text: They mistake a person being online for a person being available to them.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds like a design problem.

lines.speaker: Ren Okafor
lines.text: The button is green. Apparently that is a binding philosophical argument.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you tell them?

lines.speaker: Ren Okafor
lines.text: Green is a color. Ask a question.

topics.label: Explain the service fee.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The fee has a fee under it.

lines.speaker: Ren Okafor
lines.text: That’s the fee-recognition fee. It helps the first fee feel seen.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You’re joking.

lines.speaker: Ren Okafor
lines.text: Yes. The frightening part is how long you needed to check.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Could you write the app copy?

lines.speaker: Ren Okafor
lines.text: I tried putting WE DO NOT KNOW YET on a button. They said it lacked confidence.

topics.label: What happens after the shift?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You sound like you could do this all night.

lines.speaker: Ren Okafor
lines.text: I sound professional. Those are different schedules.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s waiting after work?

lines.speaker: Ren Okafor
lines.text: Tasha’s radio draft, a quiet meal, and a phone I’m allowed to ignore.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does Nadia actually let you leave?

lines.speaker: Ren Okafor
lines.text: Yes. Then she answers three more calls. We’re working on her ending too.

dialogue.farewell: Agreement before assumption. It saves everyone an entire conversation.

npcs.name: Mike Hawk
npcs.backstory: Mike has spent most of his adult life turning small public appearances into occasions. He remembers shop openings, waits for cameras, and has a remarkable ability to make a basic promise sound like an intimate threat. He is not secretly a policy genius or only a walking name joke: he does care that the block’s broken pavement keeps hurting local trade, and he dislikes the patient work needed to fix it. Ada knows he listens better without a microphone. Noah suspects he could be useful if he would read his own briefing. Mike’s immediate goal is to earn one endorsement for something he actually completes. His temptation is to substitute another memorable line for that completion and trust everyone to applaud before asking when.
npcs.personality: Genial, vain, shameless with wordplay; capable of sincerity when the performance pauses.

dialogue.greeting: Mike Hawk. A name you can stand behind. Preferably where the camera can see us.

topics.label: Give me your campaign pitch.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What can Mike Hawk do for this city?

lines.speaker: Mike Hawk
lines.text: I stand with my people long and hard on these topics.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Which topics?

lines.speaker: Mike Hawk
lines.text: The big ones. The difficult ones. The ones nobody else wants to touch.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Could you name one?

lines.speaker: Mike Hawk
lines.text: Potholes. I am deeply committed to filling the holes in this community.

topics.label: What is the actual pothole plan?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: No slogans. What happens to the broken pavement?

lines.speaker: Mike Hawk
lines.text: We log the locations, rank urgent repairs, and publish when crews are scheduled.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That was almost a normal answer.

lines.speaker: Mike Hawk
lines.text: Noah wrote it. I’m trying to respect his process.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can you promise a date?

lines.speaker: Mike Hawk
lines.text: A date, yes. An intimate relationship with the asphalt, no. Ada told me to stop saying that.

topics.label: Can you finish what you start?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: People say your promises are bigger than your results.

lines.speaker: Mike Hawk
lines.text: My commitment has impressive reach.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: There. You did it again.

lines.speaker: Mike Hawk
lines.text: Fair. Mara wants her loading spot clear. That is something I can help organize today.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Without a press conference?

lines.speaker: Mike Hawk
lines.text: A small one. No? All right. One completed favor. Let’s see how the body politic handles it.

dialogue.farewell: Stand with Mike Hawk. Read the platform before you repeat the slogan.

npcs.name: Ada Reyes
npcs.backstory: Ada helped organize small community events in San Juan before moving to the city. She joined Mike’s campaign because she could get people to stop walking and because she hoped the office might become useful between speeches. She carries a notebook of practical requests: a difficult curb, a blocked loading spot, a streetlight somebody keeps reporting. Her talent is delivering an outrageous line with an entirely straight face, then asking the follow-up that reveals what the neighbor really needs. She gets on well with Lin because both know the difference between a performance and a promise. Ada wants a public record of completed requests, starting with one achievable task. She is prepared to make Mike do it even if she has to take the microphone away herself.
npcs.personality: Composed, amused, persistent; uses a sales pitch to begin an honest conversation.

dialogue.greeting: I have the short pitch and the useful answer. You’re allowed to ask for both.

topics.label: Why should I stand with Mike Hawk?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why should I stand with Mike Hawk?

lines.speaker: Ada Reyes
lines.text: He offers firm support, lasting commitment, and a platform that can take the pressure.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You practiced saying that without smiling.

lines.speaker: Ada Reyes
lines.text: For twenty minutes. Then Noah asked me to explain storm drains.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can you?

lines.speaker: Ada Reyes
lines.text: Yes. That’s why they keep sending me outside instead of the candidate.

topics.label: What is in your notebook?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is that a list of potential voters?

lines.speaker: Ada Reyes
lines.text: In this campaign it’s a list of things people asked us to fix.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s at the top?

lines.speaker: Ada Reyes
lines.text: A loading space Mara can use without moving three campaign signs.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Your own signs are the problem?

lines.speaker: Ada Reyes
lines.text: Democracy occasionally begins with cleaning up your own bullshit.

topics.label: You and Lin seem friendly.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You keep passing people to the tea shop.

lines.speaker: Ada Reyes
lines.text: A person can have civic opinions and be thirsty.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does Mike approve?

lines.speaker: Ada Reyes
lines.text: He asked whether the cup could carry his face.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What did Mara say?

lines.speaker: Ada Reyes
lines.text: She asked whether the face would help the kettle boil. The negotiations are ongoing.

dialogue.farewell: If you want a promise written down, find me before Mike finds a camera.

npcs.name: Noah Bennett
npcs.backstory: Noah wrote explanatory material in Bristol and moved to the city believing he could make public decisions less exhausting to understand. He accepted Mike’s campaign job because the candidate could hold an audience that would otherwise walk away. He did not anticipate seeing a paragraph about road maintenance reduced to a poster about endurance. Noah is funny in a quieter way than his employer: he reads the slogan aloud, waits, and lets the absurdity do its work. He keeps earlier drafts because revisions sometimes remove the only measurable promise. His ambition is to publish a one-page plan the neighborhood can check against reality. Ada is his ally; Mike is both the audience for his work and its most enthusiastic editor.
npcs.personality: Patient, literate, deadpan; values a promise that can be checked afterward.

dialogue.greeting: If you have a policy question, please ask it before somebody gives you a shirt.

topics.label: Did you write those slogans?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did you write LONG AND HARD ON THE ISSUES?

lines.speaker: Noah Bennett
lines.text: I wrote a paragraph about durable road surfaces and sustained funding.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Then what happened?

lines.speaker: Noah Bennett
lines.text: Mike discovered that the printer charges by the page and charisma charges by the omission.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you keep the original?

lines.speaker: Noah Bennett
lines.text: Several copies. One day an archaeologist will find out we had a drainage policy.

topics.label: How do you judge a promise?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What makes a campaign promise useful?

lines.speaker: Noah Bennett
lines.text: You should know what would count as doing it and when to check.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Mike promises strong support.

lines.speaker: Noah Bennett
lines.text: Very difficult to measure with a clipboard.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So ask him for something specific?

lines.speaker: Noah Bennett
lines.text: Yes. A cleared loading space would be an excellent first date with accountability.

topics.label: What is on page two?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why does your poster say PLEASE READ PAGE TWO?

lines.speaker: Noah Bennett
lines.text: Page one has Mike’s face. Page two explains where the money is meant to go.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Which one gets photographed?

lines.speaker: Noah Bennett
lines.text: The face. It has fewer footnotes and a stronger relationship with ring lights.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why stay?

lines.speaker: Noah Bennett
lines.text: Because Ada remembers every request, and occasionally Mike listens. I would like to build on that occasion.

dialogue.farewell: Take the policy sheet. It folds more easily than the candidate admits.

npcs.name: June Park
npcs.backstory: June started cataloguing secondhand clothing in Toronto and discovered that an ordinary receipt can puncture an extraordinary sales pitch. She came to the city for a retail opportunity and stayed because the neighborhood’s sneaker stories never seemed to end at the same place twice. She opened the Exchange with a condition report, a pencil, and an insistence that a replica is allowed to be good without pretending to be original. She does not dismiss the Robbery 1s story; she refuses to turn uncertainty into a surcharge. Samira helps her keep the accounts distinct, while Leo reminds her that shoes can be useful even when their paperwork is a mess. June wants one exhibit that shows what is known, who said it, and where the gaps remain.
npcs.personality: Skeptical without sneering, patient with evidence, impatient with inflated certainty.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome. If you brought a story, I’ll ask who told you. If you brought shoes, I’ll check the soles.

topics.label: Are those the actual Robbery 1s?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is that the original pair?

lines.speaker: June Park
lines.text: Read the label. Clearly Labeled Replica 1s.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That is aggressively clear.

lines.speaker: June Park
lines.text: It needs to survive a customer saying, But I thought.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So where is the original?

lines.speaker: June Park
lines.text: I won’t claim to have it just because an empty display looks less impressive. A good story is no excuse for a bad label.

topics.label: What would convince you?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Would you believe a curse if everybody told the same story?

lines.speaker: June Park
lines.text: I’d ask whether they all heard it from the same person.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You make this sound unromantic.

lines.speaker: June Park
lines.text: A receipt can be romantic. It says somebody remembered a date and made a commitment.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And a missing receipt?

lines.speaker: June Park
lines.text: That says we have more questions. It does not automatically say haunted.

topics.label: What are those names on the board?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The Drop Watch and Designer Kicks share this counter?

lines.speaker: June Park
lines.text: They share space on the noticeboard. The Drop Watch keeps the release gossip moving; Designer Kicks gets people arguing about style.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What does The Drop Watch cover?

lines.speaker: June Park
lines.text: The moment a release becomes a personality contest.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And your job?

lines.speaker: June Park
lines.text: Make sure the thing in the box is still described correctly after the personality leaves.

dialogue.farewell: Keep the receipt. It is the quietest character in a very loud story.

npcs.name: Leo Mercer
npcs.backstory: Leo learned to repair shoes in Detroit because replacing every worn pair was beyond his budget. What began as necessity became a craft he enjoys: stitching that holds, balanced repairs, and the moment someone recognizes a favorite pair again. He joined June’s shop hoping to be known for that work. Instead people keep asking whether the glue can stop a curse. He answers with a joke, then shows them the repair anyway. Leo is the youngest new employee in the district but has no desire to play the reckless apprentice. He wants a small demonstration bench where customers can watch a patient process. His friendship with Tomas rests on a shared frustration: everyone applauds the reveal and forgets the maintenance that made it possible.
npcs.personality: Warm, practical, proud of craft; enjoys jokes without endorsing every legend.

dialogue.greeting: I can fix the sole. If you mean the other kind of soul, Samira has a longer conversation ready.

topics.label: Can you repair cursed shoes?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can you take a curse out of a sneaker?

lines.speaker: Leo Mercer
lines.text: I can take a nail out of one. Let’s start with the documented problem.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: June doesn’t believe the stories either?

lines.speaker: Leo Mercer
lines.text: June believes you told her a story. That’s different from certifying it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And you?

lines.speaker: Leo Mercer
lines.text: I believe these stitches need doing before the next dramatic entrance.

topics.label: How did you learn this?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why repair shoes instead of chasing every new drop?

lines.speaker: Leo Mercer
lines.text: Because I liked the pair I had, and the new pair liked money I didn’t have.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So you taught yourself?

lines.speaker: Leo Mercer
lines.text: With help, mistakes, and one repair I will never photograph.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Would you show someone else?

lines.speaker: Leo Mercer
lines.text: Absolutely. Watching a thing get fixed is a better flex than pretending it never broke.

topics.label: You know Tomas next door?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Tomas says you understand his problems.

lines.speaker: Leo Mercer
lines.text: He makes vehicles ready for the camera. I make shoes ready for the pavement.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Same job?

lines.speaker: Leo Mercer
lines.text: Different invoices. Same customer asking whether the glue can dry faster because they’re late.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can it?

lines.speaker: Leo Mercer
lines.text: Urgency is a feeling. Drying is a process. They have never signed a cooperation agreement.

dialogue.farewell: Walk carefully until it sets. Confidence is not a substitute for drying time.

npcs.name: Samira Diallo
npcs.backstory: Samira grew up in Dakar loving the way different people could remember the same event without telling the same story. She later worked on small print projects and came to the city to make an oral-history zine. The Robbery 1s legend attracted her because people revealed as much about themselves as about the shoes. She works at the Exchange to record those versions without flattening them into one convenient advertisement. She can enjoy an extravagant tale and still ask when the speaker was actually present. Her first issue keeps spaces for unresolved details rather than filling them with invented certainty. June values that restraint. Samira’s private challenge is that an unanswered question sells fewer copies than a shocking conclusion.
npcs.personality: Curious, vivid, discerning; likes a great story enough to preserve its uncertainty.

dialogue.greeting: Tell me the version you heard. Start with who told you, not with trust me.

topics.label: Which version is true?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who wore the shoes first?

lines.speaker: Samira Diallo
lines.text: That depends which version somebody is trying to sell you. Let me find the account before I give you a confident name.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: But you keep everyone’s version?

lines.speaker: Samira Diallo
lines.text: I keep who said it and what they claimed. A rumor deserves quotation marks.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does that ruin the fun?

lines.speaker: Samira Diallo
lines.text: No. Sometimes the difference between two stories is the most interesting part.

topics.label: Why call the zine Unconfirmed?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: UNCONFIRMED is a strange title for something you want me to buy.

lines.speaker: Samira Diallo
lines.text: It’s a very accurate description of what I am selling.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Hugo would put SHOCKING TRUTH on it.

lines.speaker: Samira Diallo
lines.text: Hugo would sponsor the word shocking and invoice the truth separately.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Will the next issue have answers?

lines.speaker: Samira Diallo
lines.text: It will have better questions if I’m doing my work properly.

topics.label: Am I part of the curse now?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: If I buy the replica, am I in the story?

lines.speaker: Samira Diallo
lines.text: You’re in a story about buying a replica.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: No sudden legend attached?

lines.speaker: Samira Diallo
lines.text: If June sold you an original with that much history, the receipt would need a second page.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s almost disappointing.

lines.speaker: Samira Diallo
lines.text: Live a little. Give me something worth writing down that isn’t a receipt misunderstanding.

dialogue.farewell: If the story changes, bring the reason it changed.

npcs.name: Vik Rao
npcs.backstory: Vik began on small production crews in Bengaluru, carrying equipment and learning how much a scene depends on the person who arrives early with the right adapter. In the city he found that the same practical advice sounded more impressive when delivered like a mission briefing. Hitman Gear grew from that running joke. He takes the craft seriously while enjoying a presentation that treats finding an outlet as a strategic breakthrough. Marisol stops him promising wardrobe miracles; Owen knows when to puncture the mood with an embarrassingly ordinary sound prop. Vik wants to produce one beautifully simple commercial using the equipment they already own. His weakness is the temptation to make the preparation more dramatic than the finished scene.
npcs.personality: Precise, theatrical, generous with practical knowledge; occasionally intoxicated by his own briefing.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome to Hitman Gear. State your scene, your budget, and whether anyone remembered batteries.

topics.label: Why does buying a clapboard feel dangerous?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why are you whispering about a lighting stand?

lines.speaker: Vik Rao
lines.text: Because this stand is the difference between a sinister silhouette and a man beside a lamp.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Couldn’t you just say that normally?

lines.speaker: Vik Rao
lines.text: I tried. Nobody remembered the adapter.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do they remember it now?

lines.speaker: Vik Rao
lines.text: No. But they forget with a much more professional posture.

topics.label: What does the Plot Armor do?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does the Plot Armor vest protect me?

lines.speaker: Vik Rao
lines.text: From an uninteresting silhouette. Marisol handles the fit.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Anything else?

lines.speaker: Vik Rao
lines.text: It is a costume, not a miracle. I prefer customers who remain clear on the difference.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why call it Plot Armor?

lines.speaker: Vik Rao
lines.text: Because Unnecessarily Confident Vest was too accurate for Hugo’s ad copy.

topics.label: Who actually saved the shoot?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: RealCameraMen says they saved the commercial.

lines.speaker: Vik Rao
lines.text: They did. We lit it. Owen made the sound. Cleo directed it. Kwame kept everyone fed.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds like a team.

lines.speaker: Vik Rao
lines.text: Please don’t say that too loudly. We have an entire promotional feud to maintain.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What did you personally contribute?

lines.speaker: Vik Rao
lines.text: The adapter. History eventually returns to the adapter.

dialogue.farewell: Check the case before you leave. The dramatic reveal should not be an empty compartment.

npcs.name: Marisol Vega
npcs.backstory: Marisol learned alterations around family celebrations in Ponce and later worked on outfits meant to survive long evenings, quick changes, and people moving unpredictably. After arriving in the city she discovered that film wardrobe involves the same demands with more people using the word vision. She joined Vik because he would give a practical repair the same solemn attention as an expensive new purchase. She designs the shop’s fictional Plot Armor costume as a joke about confidence, never as protective equipment. Marisol wants repeat clients who return garments in one piece and tell her what actually happened on set. Her friendship with Beatrice is built on a shared refusal to let glamorous branding erase the people doing careful work behind it.
npcs.personality: Direct, inventive, observant; laughs at grand poses while respecting real effort.

dialogue.greeting: Turn around once before you tell me it fits. Confidence has hidden a lot of bad tailoring.

topics.label: Can you make me look important?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can this outfit make me look like I run things?

lines.speaker: Marisol Vega
lines.text: It can fit. The rest depends on whether you know where you’re going.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Vik promised presence.

lines.speaker: Marisol Vega
lines.text: Vik can create presence with a table lamp. I work with shoulders.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is that a yes?

lines.speaker: Marisol Vega
lines.text: It’s a yes to the fitting. Don’t embroider a promotion onto it.

topics.label: Why does Plot Armor have a return date?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why put a return date on Plot Armor?

lines.speaker: Marisol Vega
lines.text: Because every main character thinks the costume becomes theirs when the camera turns off.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What if the plot needs it longer?

lines.speaker: Marisol Vega
lines.text: Then the plot can call before Friday.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You’ve said that before.

lines.speaker: Marisol Vega
lines.text: To a man wearing my jacket in an interview about his signature personal style.

topics.label: What did Beatrice order?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Beatrice says you understand her brand.

lines.speaker: Marisol Vega
lines.text: She wanted a jacket she could dispatch in all day and still wear on camera.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So you made it glamorous?

lines.speaker: Marisol Vega
lines.text: I gave it pockets where her hands actually go. Then we chose the color.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s the secret?

lines.speaker: Marisol Vega
lines.text: The person has to live in the thing. The advertisement only borrows it.

dialogue.farewell: Keep the garment bag. It has done nothing to deserve being abandoned.

npcs.name: Owen Price
npcs.backstory: Owen worked on small theatre and audio projects in Cardiff, where a carefully timed ordinary noise could persuade a room to imagine something enormous. He moved to the city with a collection of practical sound tricks and no desire to pretend the objects themselves were magical. At Hitman Gear he builds ominous effects from harmless household props, then spoils his own mystique by showing how mundane the setup looks. He and Vik enjoy the same joke from opposite ends: Vik builds tension, Owen reveals the biscuit tin. Owen wants a listening event where people judge a scene before seeing the equipment. He is quietly sensitive about credit because sound is often the first thing praised vaguely and the last contribution named correctly.
npcs.personality: Dry, patient, mischievous; cares deeply about listening and accurate credits.

dialogue.greeting: If you heard something expensive, it was probably an inexpensive object in the next room.

topics.label: What made that dramatic noise?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounded like a huge metal door.

lines.speaker: Owen Price
lines.text: Biscuit tin. Slightly damaged. Very committed performance.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Seriously?

lines.speaker: Owen Price
lines.text: The door you imagined had a larger budget than the door we could afford.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does telling me ruin it?

lines.speaker: Owen Price
lines.text: Only if you think imagination comes with a purchase receipt.

topics.label: Who did the shoot?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who did the shoot?

lines.speaker: Owen Price
lines.text: Several people. Who did the sound is a question I hear less often.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You did the sound?

lines.speaker: Owen Price
lines.text: Yes. You noticed it, which means we are already having a very good day.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What credit do you want?

lines.speaker: Owen Price
lines.text: My name in the right place. Not thanks to everyone, followed by four paragraphs about the lens.

topics.label: Why sell a Silence on Set badge?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does that badge make people quiet?

lines.speaker: Owen Price
lines.text: No. It makes the moment they ignore you look official.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Ever managed complete silence here?

lines.speaker: Owen Price
lines.text: Once. Mike paused before a speech and Mara’s kettle had finished.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How long did it last?

lines.speaker: Owen Price
lines.text: Long enough for Hugo to ask whether silence had a sponsor.

dialogue.farewell: Listen to the street on your way out. It has a more honest soundtrack than the ads.

npcs.name: Zofia Nowak
npcs.backstory: Zofia trained on practical camera work in Łódź and spent enough productions solving mundane problems to distrust equipment worship. Her RealCameraMen persona deliberately says the opposite with a straight face: a lens becomes a moral position, a memory card becomes a test of character, and a battery failure becomes artistic intent. Off camera she recommends what fits the job and budget. She wants the joke to reward people who recognize the contradiction rather than mislead newcomers. Cleo can tell when a monologue needs cutting. Kwame can tell when another unpaid take is eating the lunch break. Zofia’s ongoing irritation is a client crediting whoever happened to stand nearest the camera.
npcs.personality: Deadpan, capable, skeptical of gear status; sharply separates her comic persona from practical advice.

dialogue.greeting: Before I judge your lens as a joke, tell me what you actually need to film.

topics.label: Give me a RealCameraMen rule.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What is today’s equipment rule?

lines.speaker: Zofia Nowak
lines.text: RealCameraMen never change batteries. We wait until the camera respects the schedule.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds impossible.

lines.speaker: Zofia Nowak
lines.text: Good. You have identified the comic persona.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What is the actual advice?

lines.speaker: Zofia Nowak
lines.text: Charge the batteries and label them. It works beautifully and ruins the monologue.

topics.label: Is the expensive lens always better?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Will a more expensive lens fix my scene?

lines.speaker: Zofia Nowak
lines.text: In the advertisement, yes. It will also repair your childhood and negotiate the invoice.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And at this counter?

lines.speaker: Zofia Nowak
lines.text: Tell me about the light, the space, and the shot. Then we can stop shopping at your anxiety.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You sound reasonable now.

lines.speaker: Zofia Nowak
lines.text: Keep it down. We have a reputation for unreasonable confidence.

topics.label: Who gets credit for the image?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who did the shoot?

lines.speaker: Zofia Nowak
lines.text: Cleo directed, I operated, Vik lit, Owen recorded, and Kwame kept it happening.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The client thanked the camera brand.

lines.speaker: Zofia Nowak
lines.text: The camera brand did not carry the cases down the stairs.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you want instead?

lines.speaker: Zofia Nowak
lines.text: An accurate credit and a paid invoice. My demands become less mysterious when written down.

dialogue.farewell: Make the picture you need. The loudest equipment opinion is rarely in it.

npcs.name: Cleo Baptiste
npcs.origin: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago
npcs.backstory: Cleo began directing short local performances in Port of Spain and became interested in the difference between a person being funny and a camera allowing the joke to land. She moved to the city for production work and found an entire commercial block that behaved like a cast. At RealCameraMen she shapes Zofia’s stern equipment rants and helps small shops turn vague ambitions into shootable scenes. She loves surprise when it reveals character and hates surprise when it means a client secretly changed the job. Mara’s tea commercial and Mike’s campaign give her recurring exercises in controlling tone without sanding off personality. Her private ambition is a quiet scene between ordinary people; everyone currently hiring her wants a bigger explosion of attention.
npcs.personality: Playful, perceptive, decisive; notices pauses, interruptions, and the moment a performance becomes honest.

dialogue.greeting: You have an idea. Good. Tell me what happens in the scene before you tell me it should feel expensive.

topics.label: Why is the tea commercial so funny?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why does Mara’s guarantee land every time?

lines.speaker: Cleo Baptiste
lines.text: Because she sounds like she means the nice part right up until the other part arrives.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So you make it louder?

lines.speaker: Cleo Baptiste
lines.text: Sometimes I make it quieter. A pause lets the audience do some work.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Mara says the zoom was an accident.

lines.speaker: Cleo Baptiste
lines.text: It was. Keeping it was a decision. Both can be true.

topics.label: How is Mike’s campaign shoot going?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can you make Mike look sincere?

lines.speaker: Cleo Baptiste
lines.text: I can film him listening. First we have to convince him listening is a visible action.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What does he want?

lines.speaker: Cleo Baptiste
lines.text: A heroic walk, a firm stance, and a long statement. You see my problem.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What would you shoot instead?

lines.speaker: Cleo Baptiste
lines.text: Ada hands him the notebook. He reads one request. Then he does it.

topics.label: What would you make for yourself?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What if nobody bought an ad for a day?

lines.speaker: Cleo Baptiste
lines.text: I’d film two people waiting for a repaired vehicle, slowly deciding to trust each other.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: No slogan?

lines.speaker: Cleo Baptiste
lines.text: No slogan. A situation. The funny part can arrive because somebody is nervous.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Sounds like the garage.

lines.speaker: Cleo Baptiste
lines.text: Exactly. That place already has a story. It doesn’t need me to shout over it.

dialogue.farewell: Come back with a situation. We can find the scene inside it.

npcs.name: Kwame Addo
npcs.backstory: Kwame organized small events in Kumasi before moving into production coordination. In the city he discovered that people who can describe a twelve-part cinematic universe sometimes struggle to name the person approving a thirty-second advertisement. He joined RealCameraMen to keep creative ideas attached to dates, meals, and agreements. He enjoys the absurdity and has his own running joke about the different denominations of exposure clients offer as payment. Still, he wants work to finish with relationships intact. His current problem is a promotional van booking that sounds suspiciously like Nadia’s and Amina’s bookings. He hopes to solve it through one shared description rather than another energetic phone call. He is saving time for a small film that does not expand every time somebody says one more thing.
npcs.personality: Organized, sociable, wry; protects time and collaboration without treating imagination as the enemy.

dialogue.greeting: Before we discuss the cinematic universe, who approves the invoice?

topics.label: Why does everyone mention deposits?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The client says the deposit is absurd.

lines.speaker: Kwame Addo
lines.text: The client requested three locations, two nights, and payment in future opportunities.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How much is an opportunity worth?

lines.speaker: Kwame Addo
lines.text: Try feeding a crew with one. Tell me which aisle stocks them.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Could you make the job smaller?

lines.speaker: Kwame Addo
lines.text: Yes. That’s a useful conversation. Free and unlimited is not a smaller job.

topics.label: Why does a small ad take so long?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: It’s only a thirty-second ad.

lines.speaker: Kwame Addo
lines.text: Correct. Now count the twelve things somebody wants to happen inside it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You can cut a few.

lines.speaker: Kwame Addo
lines.text: I did. They called back with a prequel.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What did you say?

lines.speaker: Kwame Addo
lines.text: Finish the tea commercial. Then earn the right to build the tea cinematic universe.

topics.label: Which van did you book?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did you book the same van as Hordash?

lines.speaker: Kwame Addo
lines.text: I booked a vehicle for a promo about a booking. Nadia booked a promo vehicle for a shift.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You two should talk.

lines.speaker: Kwame Addo
lines.text: We should talk while looking at the same sentence. That is the crucial improvement.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who has the keys?

lines.speaker: Kwame Addo
lines.text: Beatrice. Notice how the person with the keys has made the fewest promises.

dialogue.farewell: Send a clear brief. It is the cheapest special effect we have.

npcs.name: Darnell Brooks
npcs.backstory: Darnell first hosted small events in Baltimore and found that he could make a room care about a person simply by giving the introduction his full attention. In the city that gift became PressureTV’s comically oversized sense of urgency. A delayed delivery becomes a developing situation; a disagreement over a kettle becomes a special report. He knows he is performing, but the neighbors sometimes hear only the alarming headline. Priya keeps him attached to what actually happened, and Hugo keeps trying to turn his pauses into sponsorship slots. Darnell wants one long interview where someone finishes a difficult story without interruption. Tasha might be that guest, if he can persuade the studio that listening has entertainment value too.
npcs.personality: Expressive, curious, easily carried away by presentation; capable of becoming a thoughtful listener.

dialogue.greeting: We are following a developing conversation. You appear to be the source.

topics.label: What is breaking today?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s the big story?

lines.speaker: Darnell Brooks
lines.text: A kettle has stopped working at a location we can currently confirm is across the street.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is anyone investigating?

lines.speaker: Darnell Brooks
lines.text: Priya asked whether it was plugged in. We are awaiting a dramatic answer.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Was it?

lines.speaker: Darnell Brooks
lines.text: No. An ordinary resolution has struck this developing situation.

topics.label: Who do you want to interview?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who would you give the whole programme to?

lines.speaker: Darnell Brooks
lines.text: Tasha. She has stories about working this block that don’t need my voice over them.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Could you stay quiet that long?

lines.speaker: Darnell Brooks
lines.text: That is an unkind but relevant production question.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What would you ask first?

lines.speaker: Darnell Brooks
lines.text: What do people assume before they let you speak? Then I’d try not to demonstrate the problem.

topics.label: Do you make everything too big?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: This block is smaller than your headlines.

lines.speaker: Darnell Brooks
lines.text: A small event can matter very much to the person inside it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s a good answer. What about the ominous music?

lines.speaker: Darnell Brooks
lines.text: Owen gave me a biscuit-tin sound and I exercised insufficient restraint.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can you report something quietly?

lines.speaker: Darnell Brooks
lines.text: Yes. But you will have to lean in. That might be an improvement.

dialogue.farewell: Stay with the story. You are allowed to turn down the volume.

npcs.name: Priya Nair
npcs.backstory: Priya worked on modest media projects in Kochi where the person making the schedule also had to check the names, dates, and final edit. She brought that habit to the city’s PressureTV studio. She likes entertainment and thinks accuracy makes a joke sharper because the audience knows where the exaggeration begins. Her desk holds a corrections board that she refuses to hide behind Hugo’s advertising easel. She makes room for Diamond Girls Radio’s Nigeria/Ghana-focused programming without letting Hugo improvise facts about its guests. The PRIM3.exe notes remain on her desk because she would rather leave a slot open than announce a programme nobody can describe. Priya wants the studio to publish one correction as visibly as it published the mistake. Darnell understands why; Hugo worries about the available wall space.
npcs.personality: Clear, dry, curious; insists that getting the small facts right is part of respecting the audience.

dialogue.greeting: If you heard it in the headline, I may have a slightly more accurate sentence for you.

topics.label: What are you correcting?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why is the correction board bigger than the headline board?

lines.speaker: Priya Nair
lines.text: Because the correction has to hold the context the headline left out.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does Darnell mind?

lines.speaker: Priya Nair
lines.text: He minds when I interrupt his dramatic pause with the correct street number.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you wait?

lines.speaker: Priya Nair
lines.text: No. Suspense is useful. Sending somebody to the wrong building is less useful.

topics.label: What is Diamond Girls Radio?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s Diamond Girls Radio on the programme board?

lines.speaker: Priya Nair
lines.text: Nigeria and Ghana-focused programming under the Diamond Girls x McCluster Network.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So every person in this studio comes from those places?

lines.speaker: Priya Nair
lines.text: No. Programming geography is not an employee biography. I’m from Kochi.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And PRIM3.exe?

lines.speaker: Priya Nair
lines.text: A name in the notes while its relationship gets sorted. I don’t make a schedule out of an assumption.

topics.label: Can a sponsor buy the story?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Hugo says everybody gets exclusive treatment.

lines.speaker: Priya Nair
lines.text: Hugo sells attention. I still ask what actually happened.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does that create arguments?

lines.speaker: Priya Nair
lines.text: Only on days when we are open.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why stay here?

lines.speaker: Priya Nair
lines.text: Because Darnell can make people care, and I can help him care about the right detail.

dialogue.farewell: Bring a detail you can explain. We can build a better story around it.

npcs.name: Hugo Soto
npcs.backstory: Hugo sold event advertising in Montevideo and developed a talent for making small budgets feel capable of enormous ambitions. In the city he knows every shopkeeper, remembers their preferred pitch, and occasionally promises overlapping forms of exclusivity. He is more hopeful than malicious: each conversation feels like a chance to make the whole block succeed, and the conflict arrives when the promises meet. Priya makes him specify what a sponsor actually receives. Darnell supplies a voice grand enough for his most optimistic copy. Hugo wants one district-wide commercial package that everyone understands and still wants to buy. To get there he has to admit that a genuine shared opportunity may be less flattering than telling eight businesses they each own the entire street.
npcs.personality: Effusive, inventive, persuasive; often outpaces his own ability to deliver.

dialogue.greeting: I can already see your campaign. First, tell me whether you have a campaign budget.

topics.label: Who has the exclusive sponsorship?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Mara says she has exclusive sponsorship. So does Mike.

lines.speaker: Hugo Soto
lines.text: Mara has exclusive refreshment confidence. Mike has exclusive civic firmness.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You invented those categories just now.

lines.speaker: Hugo Soto
lines.text: I clarified them just now. That is an important emotional difference.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Will they agree?

lines.speaker: Hugo Soto
lines.text: Priya says I should ask before printing anything else. I’m trying this new sequence.

topics.label: Can I pay you in exposure?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can I pay for advertising with exposure?

lines.speaker: Hugo Soto
lines.text: A cruel question to ask a man standing beside an unpaid lighting invoice.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You offered that to Tasha.

lines.speaker: Hugo Soto
lines.text: I offered an opportunity. She requested a number. Fairly, I now admit.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So what will you pay?

lines.speaker: Hugo Soto
lines.text: We are having an actual budget conversation. It has fewer sparkles and better outcomes.

topics.label: Could you write an honest ad?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Sell the whole block without promising the moon.

lines.speaker: Hugo Soto
lines.text: Eight unusual businesses. Real personalities. Something entertaining around every corner.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s good. Stop there.

lines.speaker: Hugo Soto
lines.text: And the most unprecedented—

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Hugo.

lines.speaker: Hugo Soto
lines.text: Fine. I’ll leave room for the place to surprise you. Priya will be unbearable about this.

dialogue.farewell: Think about it. I will try to let you finish thinking before the follow-up.

npcs.name: Amina Noor
npcs.backstory: Amina worked around passenger transport in Mombasa and learned that a good driver’s reputation depends on the ordinary things people notice only when they fail. She moved to the city with an interest in vehicle media and a dislike of advertising that makes responsibility look dull. Baddies on Wheels gave her room for both a polished entrance and a carefully kept schedule. She hosts the promotional pieces but does not expect a camera to excuse arriving late. Tomas handles practical vehicle preparation; Beatrice controls the bookings with a memory that humbles everybody else’s app. Amina wants their next film to show the work behind the image without losing the enjoyment. The mistaken van booking tests whether she can protect the business while staying friendly with the neighbors who helped build it.
npcs.personality: Confident, attentive, stylish, and unwilling to confuse spectacle with dependable service.

dialogue.greeting: A good entrance starts with actually arriving. You would be surprised how many ads skip that part.

topics.label: What makes the ride special?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What does Baddies on Wheels promise?

lines.speaker: Amina Noor
lines.text: Presence, personality, and somebody who remembers where you’re going.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Which part looks best on camera?

lines.speaker: Amina Noor
lines.text: The arrival. Which is why Tomas and Beatrice deserve more screen time.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You want to film dispatch?

lines.speaker: Amina Noor
lines.text: Watch Beatrice solve a bad booking in thirty seconds. That woman has action scenes.

topics.label: Who gets the promotional van?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Nadia and Kwame both think they booked your van.

lines.speaker: Amina Noor
lines.text: Then we have one vehicle and two descriptions that need improvement.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Could you just give it to the first person?

lines.speaker: Amina Noor
lines.text: I could. Or I could find out whether the times actually conflict.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds less dramatic.

lines.speaker: Amina Noor
lines.text: Good. Save the drama for the commercial. A useful answer is allowed to be quiet.

topics.label: How do you know the Whip garage?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why send people to the garage?

lines.speaker: Amina Noor
lines.text: Because a vehicle can look perfect on a screen and still need someone to listen to it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You trust the people there?

lines.speaker: Amina Noor
lines.text: I trust a clear agreement and work someone will stand behind. That is how we build a relationship.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is your pass an actual booking?

lines.speaker: Amina Noor
lines.text: It’s a souvenir. Beatrice would never let a shiny card pretend it knew her schedule.

dialogue.farewell: Enjoy the entrance. Remember the people who made it possible.

npcs.name: Tomas Silva
npcs.backstory: Tomas learned practical vehicle work in Porto and found satisfaction in problems that stopped being mysterious after someone paid close attention. In the city he prepares Baddies on Wheels’ working vehicles for their second life as media subjects. That means fitting a polished shoot into the same schedule as inspections, cleaning, and ordinary repairs. He likes the cameras when they show a finished job and dislikes requests to conceal a problem because it is out of frame. Leo at the shoe exchange understands the same argument on a smaller scale. Tomas wants to produce a short maintenance feature with Amina that is useful enough to keep and funny enough to finish watching. His immediate wish is more modest: a booking description that leaves time for the vehicle to return before the next shoot begins.
npcs.personality: Methodical, easygoing, quietly proud; respects maintenance more than magical fixes.

dialogue.greeting: If the request begins with just a quick shot, show me the schedule before the camera.

topics.label: Why are you arguing with a camera crew?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The camera only sees the left side. Why fix the other one?

lines.speaker: Tomas Silva
lines.text: Because the vehicle has to drive away with both sides afterward.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That was the producer’s question.

lines.speaker: Tomas Silva
lines.text: Then send the producer this answer. I can wait while you put it in a dramatic font.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does Amina back you up?

lines.speaker: Tomas Silva
lines.text: Yes. Her entrance still has to get home.

topics.label: What do you and Leo talk about?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You and Leo keep talking about drying time.

lines.speaker: Tomas Silva
lines.text: He repairs shoes. I prepare vehicles. We both meet people who think urgency changes materials.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Doesn’t a bigger budget help?

lines.speaker: Tomas Silva
lines.text: It can buy a better plan. It cannot buy yesterday.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You should put that on a shirt.

lines.speaker: Tomas Silva
lines.text: Hugo already offered. He asked whether I could have it printed yesterday.

topics.label: What would your own show be?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Would you host a maintenance segment?

lines.speaker: Tomas Silva
lines.text: With Amina, yes. Show the real problem, the useful check, and when to get proper help.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What is the joke?

lines.speaker: Tomas Silva
lines.text: Everybody expects the camera to reveal a glamorous secret. Sometimes the secret is somebody remembered the appointment.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Will people watch?

lines.speaker: Tomas Silva
lines.text: Leo says they will if we let them see a thing get better.

dialogue.farewell: Leave time for the return trip. The schedule also has to come home.

npcs.name: Beatrice Cole
npcs.role: Dispatcher and keeper of the keys
npcs.backstory: Beatrice spent years coordinating work and family trips around Bridgeport before taking a dispatch role in the fictional neighboring city. She remembers a booking because she listens to why it matters, and she remembers an unpaid favor because the person tends to ask again. The Baddies on Wheels name amuses her; she sees no age limit on arriving with style. She is the business’s calm center and occasionally its funniest person, although the younger staff are still learning when she is winding them up. Marisol makes her clothes that work through a whole shift. Amina trusts her to say no when the schedule requires it. Beatrice wants the next promotional film to show her as part of the brand rather than someone moving out of the frame before the glamorous people arrive.
npcs.personality: Unhurried, formidable, warm; carries exact memories without making every favor a debt.

dialogue.greeting: Yes, I have the keys. No, confidence is not a booking reference.

topics.label: How do you keep this straight?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Three businesses want the same van.

lines.speaker: Beatrice Cole
lines.text: Then three businesses can tell me a time, a destination, and what goes inside it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: They sent dramatic descriptions.

lines.speaker: Beatrice Cole
lines.text: Lovely. I’ll put those in the dramatic-description drawer, which is also the bin.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You sound very calm.

lines.speaker: Beatrice Cole
lines.text: The keys do not get more available when I panic.

topics.label: You are in the promo too?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You’re going to be in the next Baddies shoot?

lines.speaker: Beatrice Cole
lines.text: Was there an age limit on arriving properly dressed that somebody forgot to send me?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: No, I meant—

lines.speaker: Beatrice Cole
lines.text: I know what you meant. Marisol made the jacket. You can survive the reveal.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What is your scene?

lines.speaker: Beatrice Cole
lines.text: I open the door, look excellent, and ask whether everybody signed the vehicle back in.

topics.label: Do you remember every favor?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: People say you remember everything.

lines.speaker: Beatrice Cole
lines.text: Only the important parts. Who needed help, who turned up, and who called being late a personal brand.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you hold it against them?

lines.speaker: Beatrice Cole
lines.text: Not forever. I like giving people a chance to become easier to rely on.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And if they don’t?

lines.speaker: Beatrice Cole
lines.text: They can enjoy a very clear answer the next time they ask for the keys.

dialogue.farewell: Get where you’re going. Let somebody know when you arrive.
